INTRODUCTION
Why safe digital finance matters
Adults with an account
Made or received a digital payment
Access
Accounts can support saving, receiving money and payments.
Digital use
Phone access and skills shape whether accounts are used digitally.
Safety
Scam calls and misleading requests may undermine trust.
Research question
How are digital payment use and reported money requests related?
2024 weighted estimates among adults aged 15+, n = 3,000.
An account is a starting point; usable and trusted services matter too.
Source: World Bank Global Findex 2025 India microdata (2024), https://doi.org/10.48529/c9vy-pq51. Estimates calculated using wgt; sample sizes unweighted.
CONCEPTS
From access to safe and confident use
1  Account
Access to a formal financial account.
2  Connectivity
Phone ownership, internet access and skills.
3  Digital use
Making or receiving digital payments.
4  Safety
Device security, fraud prevention and redress.
Why trust matters
World Bank guidance identifies awareness, safeguards and dispute resolution as contributors to confidence in digital services.
Our distinction
A phone lock protects access to a device. It does not necessarily prevent a user from authorizing a deceptive payment.
These mechanisms inform our interpretation; the survey cannot establish causality.

Source: World Bank Global Findex 2025 India microdata (2024), https://doi.org/10.48529/c9vy-pq51. Estimates calculated using wgt; sample sizes unweighted. World Bank: https://digitalfinance.worldbank.org/topics/digital-financial-literacy/trust ; https://digitalfinance.worldbank.org/topics/financial-consumer-protection.
RESEARCH DESIGN
India survey: data and method
adult respondents
phone owners
interview year
reported requests
Measures

Account and payment indicators: all adults.

Device lock and request exposure: phone owners.

Sent money: only those reporting a request.
Analysis

Weighted proportions and group comparisons.

Weighted logistic model adjusts for demographics.

A focused review interprets institutional guidance.
All counts are unweighted; percentages use the survey weight.
The survey is cross-sectional and self-reported; no cause-and-effect claim is made.

Interpretation
Access alone does not guarantee digital use. Device access, confidence, affordability and preferences may all play a role.

FINDING 3
Payment use and reported unsolicited requests
Request rate among phone-owning payment users versus non-users.
Read this carefully
An unknown person asking for money is not necessarily a scam. The difference may reflect other factors and cannot establish causality.
Users n = 1,283; non-users n = 862. Weighted percentages.
The 8.8-point difference is an association, not a measure of fraud losses.
Source: World Bank Global Findex 2025 India microdata (2024), https://doi.org/10.48529/c9vy-pq51. Estimates calculated using wgt; sample sizes unweighted.
FINDING 4
An adjusted association, with limits
Adjusted odds ratio for payment users.
Approximate 95% interval.
Phone owners in the model.
Model controls
Gender, age, education, income quintile, workforce participation and rural/urban residence.
Uncertainty and interpretation
Odds ratios are not relative risks. The public file lacks full survey design identifiers, so intervals assume independent observations.
Results remain exploratory: selection and unmeasured differences can affect the association.

QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
What published guidance suggests
1  Trust and adoption
World Bank guidance connects consumer trust with awareness, safeguards and effective dispute resolution.
2  Shared responsibility
Provider safeguards and clear redress complement user education. A phone lock alone is not protection against every scam.
3  Accessible support
Gaps by gender and income suggest testing local-language guidance and low-cost-device access.
Approach: focused interpretation of World Bank and RBI materials; no interviews or focus groups were conducted.
These themes generate hypotheses to test; they are not respondent quotations.

ENTREPRENEURIAL OPPORTUNITY
A safety companion and a practical pilot
Proposed service
Short lessons in local languages, a payment checklist and verified routes to assistance. Never request a PIN or OTP.
Potential customer
A bank, payment provider or merchant network could support distribution. Demand and pricing are untested.
Pilot measures
Scenario comprehension, help-channel discovery and usability on low-cost devices.
Business test
Compare partner revenue with onboarding, content, support and infrastructure costs.
Test user demand and unintended friction before claiming commercial viability.
Source: World Bank Global Findex 2025 India microdata (2024), https://doi.org/10.48529/c9vy-pq51. Estimates calculated using wgt; sample sizes unweighted.
WRAP-UP
Takeaways, limitations and next steps
Key findings

89.0% account ownership; 48.5% digital payment use.

Phone-owning users reported more unsolicited requests.

Device-lock use differs across groups.
Limitations

Self-reported, cross-sectional adult survey.

Requests are not verified fraud losses.

Model uncertainty is not design-based.
Next steps

Interview and test with users.

Pilot comprehension and reporting.

Seek survey-design information and study verified losses.
The strongest conclusion is a need to study safe digital use, not proof of a causal effect.
Source: World Bank Global Findex 2025 India microdata (2024), https://doi.org/10.48529/c9vy-pq51. Estimates calculated using wgt; sample sizes unweighted.
